dimensions.name: Line1_RangeSplit_and_KeyRangeImpact
dimensions.source_line: Adding token X forces the system to split the original range and rebuild the Merkle trees for the new ranges, while also locating the keys that belong to each sub-range.

criteria.excellent: Correctly explains all three elements: (1) token insertion splits the original range, (2) Merkle trees must be rebuilt, and (3) keys must be reassigned into new sub-ranges.
criteria.good: Captures most elements but omits one (e.g., mentions range split but not Merkle-tree rebuild).
criteria.poor: Describes only one element or shows partial misunderstanding of why these consequences follow.
criteria.bad: Misses or misstates the mechanism entirely.

dimensions.name: Line2_Rescan_Requirement_and_RandomTokenEffect
dimensions.source_line: Because the new ranges didn’t previously exist, the node that owned (A,B] must rescan its storage to determine which keys belong to (A,X] and which belong to (X,B]. This happens because random token placement reshapes range boundaries whenever a new node joins.

criteria.excellent: Shows that new sub-ranges have no preexisting index, forcing a full rescan, and correctly attributes this to random token placement reshaping boundaries.
criteria.good: Acknowledges rescanning or range-boundary changes but does not fully connect the reasoning.
criteria.poor: Mentions rescanning without linking it to non-existent ranges or token randomness.
criteria.bad: Fails to recognize why rescanning is needed or misattributes the cause.

dimensions.name: Line3_MerkleTree_Invalidation_and_NoReuse
dimensions.source_line: The Merkle tree associated with (A,B] no longer matches either of the new ranges, so neither subtree of the original hash structure can be reused. A fresh Merkle tree must be built for each new interval.

criteria.excellent: Accurately explains why the original Merkle tree becomes invalid, why subtree reuse is impossible, and that full reconstruction is required.
criteria.good: Correctly states that the Merkle tree must be rebuilt but gives incomplete justification.
criteria.poor: Shows confusion about Merkle-tree structure or claims partial reuse is possible without justification.
criteria.bad: Fails to understand why the old Merkle tree cannot apply or denies the need for rebuilding.

dimensions.name: Line4_BootstrapPerformanceImpact
dimensions.source_line: This slows bootstrapping significantly because the system cannot hand off accurate replicas until both the range scans and the Merkle-tree rebuilds complete.

criteria.excellent: Clearly connects rescanning + Merkle rebuild costs to slower bootstrapping and the inability to hand off correct replicas.
criteria.good: Identifies that performance is slowed but only loosely links it to the required operations.
criteria.poor: Mentions slowdown without tying it to accuracy requirements or the dependency on completed rebuilds.
criteria.bad: Does not recognize any performance impact or incorrectly attributes it.
